from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

Let $1\le i\le n-2$, put $s:=s_i$, $t:=s_{i+1}$ and write
$B_iB_{i+1}B_i:=B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i$. Then there are degree-zero
isomorphisms of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_i,\qquad B_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_{i+1},$$
with no additional grading shift on any summand, where $B_{i,i+1,i}$ is the
rank-two longest bimodule of
[[def-the-rank-two-longest-type-a-soergel-bimodule]]. On split Grothendieck
classes the two decompositions read $[B_iB_{i+1}B_i]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_i]$ and
$[B_{i+1}B_iB_{i+1}]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_{i+1}]$.

**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric form that is $S$-bilinear for the right action and invariant under
the left action in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.

derivations.claim: **The character of the two-letter product.** By [F1] and multiplicativity, $\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_t)=(H_s+v)(H_t+v)=H_sH_t+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$; since $st$ is reduced, [F2] gives $H_sH_t=H_{st}$, so the standard-basis expansion is $H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$. Its coefficients give the multiplicities $1,1,1,1$ displayed, and reading the layers through [F1] the reduced dimension is $1+1+1+1=4$.

**The Kazhdan-Lusztig element of $st$.** Put $A:=v-v^{-1}$ and $J:=H_{st}+v(H_s+H_t)+v^2$; then $J\in H_{st}+v\mathbb Z[v]H_s+v\mathbb Z[v]H_t+v^2\mathbb Z[v]$. Since $H_s^{-1}=H_s+A$, $H_t^{-1}=H_t+A$ and $\overline{H_{st}}=H_{ts}^{-1}=H_s^{-1}H_t^{-1}=(H_s+A)(H_t+A)=H_{st}+A(H_s+H_t)+A^2$ (the last identity uses $H_sH_t=H_{st}$), applying the semilinear involution gives $\overline J=\overline{H_{st}}+v^{-1}(\overline{H_s}+\overline{H_t})+v^{-2}=H_{st}+A(H_s+H_t)+A^2+v^{-1}(H_s+H_t)+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}$, whose coefficients are $A+v^{-1}=v$ at $H_s+H_t$ and $A^2+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}=(v^2-2+v^{-2})+(2-2v^{-2})+v^{-2}=v^2$ at $H_e$; hence $\overline J=J$, and by uniqueness [F2], $J=\underline H_{st}$.

**Indecomposability of $B_sB_t$.** The unshifted tensor $M=S\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^t}S$ is generated as a bimodule by $1\otimes1\otimes1$. To see this, write a middle polynomial as $h_0+x_1h_1$ with $h_0,h_1\in S^s$, which slide to the first slot. The remaining $x_1$ slides to the last slot because $t=s_2$ fixes $x_1$. Therefore every tensor is a sum of $p(1\otimes1\otimes1)q$. After the shift $(2)$ its lowest component is one-dimensional in degree $-2$, by its finite left tensor basis and $S_0=\mathbb R$. A degree-zero bimodule endomorphism must send the generator to a scalar multiple of itself, and generation forces that same scalar on all of $M$. Hence its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, with no nontrivial idempotent, so $B_sB_t$ is indecomposable. The balanced map $p\otimes q\otimes r\mapsto p\,s(q)\,st(r)$ is surjective onto the $st$ graph bimodule, showing that this indecomposable has the top graph of its reduced word; it is the normalized summand $B_{st}$. Thus $B_sB_t\cong B_{st}$ with no lower summands, independently of the Hom formula.

**The three-letter braid relation.** By multiplicativity and the products computed in steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_tB_s)=\underline H_s\underline H_t\underline H_s=\underline H_{st}\underline H_s$; expanding with the Hecke relations gives $\underline H_{st}\underline H_s=\underline H_{sts}+\underline H_s$ Indeed the expansion is $J_0+H_s+v$ where $J_0=H_{sts}+v(H_{st}+H_{ts})+v^2(H_s+H_t)+v^3$. The element $J_0=\underline H_{st}\underline H_s-\underline H_s$ is bar fixed, with triangular lower coefficients in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, so uniqueness in [F2] identifies it with $\underline H_{sts}$. The reduced dimensions add to $6+2=8$. This verifies the example.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a

$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the

   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule

   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so

upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's

derivations.claim: A finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra and the absence of nontrivial idempotents imply locality. Indeed for an endomorphism $f$ its polynomial minimal relation splits into a power of $T$ and a factor coprime to $T$. The polynomial Chinese remainder identity produces an idempotent separating the nilpotent and invertible parts; indecomposability forces one part to vanish. Thus every $f$ is invertible or nilpotent, and a nonunit $f$ has $1-f$ invertible. Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction.

Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness.

Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture.

Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer.

Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$.

works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations

descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of

idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite

idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the

[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same

$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$

   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);

   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;

   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Indeed, $(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}$ is positive
exactly when $w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1)$, the left-ascent criterion for inversion
length. Thus the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The reduced module $\overline{B_x^R}$ has bottom degree
$-\ell(x)$ and top degree $+\ell(x)$; the unreduced bimodule has nonzero
components in arbitrarily high degrees. On a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

**The setting.** Keep $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$, the
place-permutation action of $S_n$, the balanced roots
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$ with $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$ and the
graded $(R,R)$-bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]; recall that
$1\otimes1\in B_i$ has degree $-1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$ has degree $1$, that
$B_i$ is generated as an $(R,R)$-bimodule by $1\otimes1$, and that $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ with
$s_i(\alpha_i)=-\alpha_i$
([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]],
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]).

**The positive generator complex.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ let $F_i$ be the
bounded cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i:=\bigl[\;B_i\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_i\ }R(1)\;\bigr],$$
with $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$, $R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and
all other terms zero, where $\varepsilon_i:B_i\to R(1)$ is the
multiplication map $\varepsilon_i(r\otimes r')=rr'$, i.e. the degree-zero
bimodule map determined by $\varepsilon_i(1\otimes1)=1$ and
$\varepsilon_i(1\otimes\alpha_i)=\alpha_i$.

**The negative generator complex.** Let $F_i^{-1}$ be the bounded cochain
complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i^{-1}:=\bigl[\;R(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta_i\ }B_i\;\bigr],$$
with $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$, $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$ and
all other terms zero, where $\eta_i:R(-1)\to B_i$ is the bimodule map
$\eta_i(1)=\alpha_i\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_i$.

**Well-definedness of the differentials.** The map $\varepsilon_i$ descends
from the multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$ because
$\varepsilon_i(ra\otimes r')=rar'=\varepsilon_i(r\otimes ar')$ for $a\in R^{s_i}$
and $R$ is commutative; it is left and right $R$-linear and homogeneous of
degree zero, since $1\otimes1\mapsto1$ matches the degrees $-1$ of $B_i$ and of
the generator of $R(1)$, and $1\otimes\alpha_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ matches the
degree $1=\deg(\alpha_i)-1$ on both sides. For $\eta_i$, the bimodule map
$R\to B_i$ sending $1$ to the class of $x_i-x'_{i+1}$ is well defined: the
products $(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_i-x'_i)$ and
$(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_{i+1}-x'_{i+1})$ vanish in $B_i$ by the explicit computation
of GKS Lemma 3.8, while for $a\notin\{i,i+1\}$ the factor $x_a-x'_a$ is already
a defining relation of $B_i$, so the element annihilates the kernel ideal of the
multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$, and the assignment $1\mapsto x_i-x'_{i+1}$
extends to a well-defined $R$-bimodule map. The value of that map at $1$ times
the unit $2\varepsilon_i$ is $\eta_i(1)$, because
$$1\otimes(x_i-x_{i+1})+(x_i-x_{i+1})\otimes1=2(x_i-x'_{i+1})$$
in $B_i$ (GKS Lemma 3.8, using $x_i+x_{i+1}=x'_i+x'_{i+1}$) and
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$; a unit multiple of a well-defined
bimodule map is a well-defined bimodule map, so $\eta_i$ is well defined. Its
value $\eta_i(1)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$, matching the degree of
$1\in R(-1)$, so $\eta_i$ is a degree-zero bimodule map. Both complexes are
concentrated in two adjacent cohomological
degrees, so $d^2=0$ holds trivially and each of $F_i,F_i^{-1}$ is a bounded
cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules in the sense of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]].

**Size and consequences.** The bimodules $R$, $R(1)$ and $R(-1)$ are free of
rank one on both sides and $B_i$ is free of rank two on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]], the bases
being $\{1\otimes1,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ on the left and
$\{1\otimes1,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ on the right). Every term of $F_i$ and of
$F_i^{-1}$ is therefore finite free, hence finite graded projective, as a left
$R$-module and as an underlying right $R$-module. Applying
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]]
with the commutative ring $\mathbb Q$ and $A=B=R$: the signed totalization with
$F_i$ is an exact triangulated functor on bounded complexes of finite graded
projective $R$-modules, preserves quasi-isomorphisms between bounded complexes,
and descends to the derived tensor functor $F_i\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}-$ on
$D^b(R\text{-grmod})$; the same statements hold with $F_i^{-1}$ in place of
$F_i$. The right-tensor construction $-\otimes_RF_i$ is defined separately by
signed totalization, and its derived version uses the same two-sided
freeness. Commutativity of $R$ does not assert a symmetry between tensor
products of arbitrary $(R,R)$-bimodules.

**Recorded convention.** The complex $F_i$ is the library normalization of
Rouquier's positive complex $F_s=[A\otimes_{A^s}A\to A]$, in which $A$ sits in
degree $1$ and the differential is multiplication: in the library external
shift $(r)$ with $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$ one has $F_i=T_i(1)$ and
$F_i^{-1}\cong T_i^{-1}(-1)$ for the GKS complexes
$T_i=[B_i(-1)\to R]$, $T_i^{-1}=[R\to B_i(1)]$ of formula (3.3). The GKS negative differential sends $1$ to
$x_i-x'_{i+1}$, whereas ours is $2\varepsilon_i$ times that map.
The chain isomorphism $F_i^{-1}\to T_i^{-1}(-1)$ is multiplication by
$2\varepsilon_i$ in degree $-1$ and the identity in degree $0$.
The internal shifts cancel in inverse pairs and agree on the two sides of
each positive braid relation. The sign $\varepsilon_i$
in $\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$, and with it the sign of $\eta_i$, is
a unit of $\mathbb Q$; the homotopy classes of the complexes do not depend on
the choice of balanced root.

**The construction.** For a signed word
$$\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},\qquad \epsilon_k\in\{\pm1\},\ 1\le i_k\le n-1,$$
put
$$F(\sigma):=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},$$
the iterated signed tensor totalization of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]] of
the Rouquier generator complexes of
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], bracketed left to
right; the empty word ($r=0$) is sent to the unit complex $R$ concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$. This is the **Rouquier complex of the word**. When
$\epsilon_k=+1$ the letter contributes the positive complex $F_{i_k}$ and when
$\epsilon_k=-1$ it contributes $F_{i_k}^{-1}$.

**Structure.** $F(\sigma)$ is a bounded cochain complex of graded
$(R,R)$-bimodules with degree-zero differentials, concentrated in cohomological
degrees $-r_-,\ldots,r_+$, where $r_-$ and $r_+$ count the negative and
positive letters: the term $F(\sigma)^m$ is the direct sum of the
$\binom{r}{m+r_-}$ tensor products of one term of each factor, since the
minimal choice has degree $-r_-$ and each upper-term choice adds one. It carries a
cohomological degree and an internal grading, and the differential is the
Koszul totalization differential. A positive letter contributes its unit term
$R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and the internal shift $(1)$ to that term; a
negative letter contributes its unit term $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$
and the internal shift $(-1)$. Every term is a finite direct sum of finite tensor products of copies
of $R(\pm1)$ and $B_i$, hence is finite free on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]), so each term
is finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module and $F(\sigma)$ defines a
derived tensor functor by
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]].

**Status of the notation.** The notation records the chosen word $(\sigma)$
together with the chosen bracket; it asserts nothing about independence of the
word, of the sign normalization or of the bracketing. That the homotopy class
of $F(\sigma)$ depends only on the braid represented by $\sigma$ is the content
of [[thm-rouquier-complex-is-well-defined-up-to-canonical-homotopy-equivalence]],
whose proof uses the braid relations of the generator complexes and could not be
stated before those relations were proved.

**Convention for comparison.** The library's positive generator $F_i$ is
Rouquier's $F_{s_i}=[A\otimes_{A^{s_i}}A\to A]$ with the library external shift
$(1)$ on both terms, after giving the polynomial variables degree $2$:
$$F_i=[(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)(1)\longrightarrow R(1)].$$
Rouquier's negative complex of §3.2.4 becomes $F_i^{-1}$ after doubling
internal degrees and shifting the whole complex by $(-1)$, up to the unit
scalar coming from the root normalization. As recorded in
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], the
complexes of Rouquier, Gorsky–Kivinen–Simental, Khovanov and Elias–Krasner
differ from $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ by homological or internal shifts, so any
comparison with those sources is read through the dictionary recorded there.
The empty word corresponds to the trivial braid and to the identity functor.

derivations.claim: **The single-factor identity.** Let $s$ be a simple reflection with root $\alpha=\alpha_s$, let $\mathrm{Br}(b):=bc_s$ on $B_s$, and let $\sigma\in S$. For every $b\in B_s$ one has $\sigma\cdot b=b\cdot(s\sigma)+\partial_s(\sigma)\,\mathrm{Br}(b)$. Indeed both sides are right $S$-linear in $b$, so it suffices to check the two basis elements: for $b=c_{\mathrm{id}}$ the identity is the rule $r\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot sr+\partial_s(r)c_s$ of [F1] with $r=\sigma$, and for $b=c_s$ it reads $\sigma\cdot c_s=c_s\cdot s\sigma+\partial_s(\sigma)c_s\alpha_s$, which is $c_s\sigma=c_s(s\sigma+\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma))$ and holds because $\sigma-s\sigma=\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma)$ and $c_s$ commutes with $S$.

**Iteration over the letters proves (a).** For $m=0$ both outer actions are multiplication by $\rho$ on $S$. For $m>0$, put $\sigma_0=\rho$ and $\sigma_i=s_i\sigma_{i-1}$. Apply step 1.1 in slot $i$ to the remainder $b_1\cdots b_{i-1}(\sigma_{i-1}b_i)b_{i+1}\cdots b_m$. This produces $\partial_{s_i}(\sigma_{i-1})\mathrm{Br}_i(b)$ and a remainder with $\sigma_i$ acting on the right of slot $i$. Balancing moves that polynomial to the left of slot $i+1$; at the last slot it is the outer right action by $x^{-1}\rho$. Each $\sigma_{i-1}$ is linear, so $\partial_{s_i}(\sigma_{i-1})=\sigma_{i-1}(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)=\gamma_i$. Also $bc_s=\mu(b)c_s$ in one factor: on $c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $c_s$ this follows from $\mu(c_{\mathrm{id}})=1$, $\mu(c_s)=\alpha_s$ and $c_s^2=c_s\alpha_s$. Thus $\mathrm{Br}_i=\chi_i\varphi_i$ with the appropriate shift of $\chi_i$, and the stated degree-two identity holds on every tensor monomial and hence on the whole bimodule.

**The covariance identity.** For all $b,b'\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ and all $i$ one has $\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_i b'\rangle=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$. It suffices to check on tensor monomials $b=b_1\cdots b_m$, $b'=b'_1\cdots b'_m$: the left side is $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots(b_ib'_ic_{s_i})\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)c_{s_i}\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)$, using $b_ic_{s_i}=\mu(b_i)c_{s_i}$ from step 2.1, so this equals $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\chi_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$, using $\operatorname{Tr}\circ\chi_i=\operatorname{Tr}_i$ and the multiplicativity of the ring structure.

**The rescaled form identity (b).** With $\varphi=\sum_i\varphi_i$ and $\langle-,-\rangle'=\bigoplus_i\langle-,-\rangle_i'$, the direct sum decomposition is orthogonal, so for all $b,b'$ one has $\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'=\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$; substituting step 3.1 gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle=\langle b,\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$, and substituting the factorization of step 2.1 gives $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle-\langle b,b'\cdot x^{-1}\rho\rangle$. The second summand is $-\langle b,b'\rangle\,x^{-1}\rho$ by right $S$-linearity of the form, and it vanishes after reduction because $x^{-1}\rho$ has positive degree; hence $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle_{\overline{\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)}}=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'$ for $b,b'$ in the reduced module, as claimed in (b).

**Positivity for reduced words and the vanished remainder (c).** Let $\underline x$ be reduced. For each $i$, the prefix $w_i:=s_{i-1}\cdots s_1$ has length $i-1$ and $s_iw_i$ has length $i$; the descent criterion [F3] therefore gives $\gamma_i=(w_i\rho)(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)>0$. All rescalings are by strictly positive real numbers, so no sign in a definite form changes; and the polynomial $x^{-1}\rho$ lies in $S_2\subset S_+$ whose right multiplication lands in $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)S_+$, which becomes zero after reduction, so the remainder vanishes on the reduced module. This proves (c).

**Identification with the Rouquier differential (d).** By [F4] the first differential of the Rouquier complex is the sum, over the letters, of the maps $\varphi_i$ from the cohomological degree $0$ term $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ to the degree $1$ term $\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)$, and its dual maps decompose the generator $c_{s_i}$ back, i.e. are the maps $\chi_i$ with the displayed internal shifts. Composing the differential with the rescaled dual maps $\gamma_i\chi_i$ and summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_i$, which by step 2.1 equals left multiplication by $\rho$ modulo the right-multiplication remainder that vanishes on the reduced module by step 5.1. Hence left multiplication by $\rho$ on the reduced Bott-Samelson module factors, up to the positive rescalings $\gamma_i$, as the composite $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)\xrightarrow{\ \gamma\chi\ }\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(2)$ built from the first Rouquier differential and its dual; all first-differential Koszul signs are $+1$, because every preceding tensor factor is in cohomological degree zero, so this is exactly $\rho\cdot(-)$ after right reduction. This proves (d) and completes the lemma; no positivity of characters and no character conjecture is used.

Let $t,u$ be signed words for the same braid $v$. Then the normalized map
$$\gamma_{t,u}\colon F(t)\longrightarrow F(u)$$
of [[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]
is a canonical homotopy equivalence, natural with respect to the multiplication
maps: for every other braid $v'$ with chosen words $t',u'$, the diagrams
comparing $F(t)\otimes_RF(t')$ with $F(u)\otimes_RF(u')$ commute up to the
canonical associativity isomorphisms, and $\gamma_{t,u}$ is the unique homotopy
class with the prescribed derived image $c_{t,u}$. Consequently the object
$G_v$ of [[thm-rouquier-complexes-form-a-coherent-braid-group-action]] is
independent of the chosen representative up to canonical homotopy equivalence,
and the notation $F(\beta)$ for the Rouquier complex of a braid element is well
defined up to canonical isomorphism in $K^b(R^e\text{-grmod})$; this is an
isomorphism statement in the homotopy category, not an equality of complexes.

**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

Let $X^\bullet$ be a cochain complex in an additive category with an
invertible-block decomposition
$d^n=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&\varphi\end{pmatrix}:A\oplus U\to B\oplus V$ and
Schur complement $\bar d=a-b\varphi^{-1}c$, as in

The kernel is $\{c_{\mathrm{id}}(-\alpha_sb)+c_sb\}=\{(c_s-c_{\mathrm{id}}\alpha_s)b\}$, so it is free of rank one as a right $S$-module with generator $c_s-c_{\mathrm{id}}\alpha_s=(\alpha_s\otimes1-1\otimes\alpha_s)/2$ of internal degree $1$; hence $\ker(\varepsilon_s)\cong S(-1)$ as a graded right $S$-module and $F_s\simeq S(-1)$ in the homotopy category of complexes of graded right $S$-modules.

**The injectivity criterion.** Let $C$ be as in (2) and let $c\in\overline{C^0}$ be homogeneous of internal degree $D$ with $\overline{d^0}(c)=0$. Then $c$ is a cocycle, so it represents a class $[c]\in H^0(\overline C)$; since $H^{-1}(\overline C)=0$ and $C^{-1}=0$, the zeroth cohomology is the cokernel of no incoming map and $[c]$ vanishes if and only if $c$ lies in the image of $\overline{d^{-1}}$, which is zero because $C^{-1}=0$. Hence $[c]\ne0$ forces $D$ to be the single internal degree $d$ in which $H^0(\overline C)$ is concentrated; therefore a nonzero kernel element can occur only in degree $d$, and the map is injective in every other degree, in particular in degrees $\le d-1$. If $C'$ is homotopy equivalent to $C$ with $C'^{-1}=0$ and is obtained by cancelling contractible two-term summands whose source lies in positive cohomological degree, then $C'^0=C^0$ for the cancellation in degrees $\ge1$, the reductions $\overline{C'}$ and $\overline C$ are homotopy equivalent by [F3], so $H^{-1}(\overline{C'})=0$ and $H^0(\overline{C'})$ is concentrated in degree $d$, and the same argument applies to $C'$. This proves (2).

**The retraction for a reduced word.** Write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$. For $m=0$ the complex is $S$. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

**The operator.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$, a strictly dominant
$\rho\in S_2$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]])
and a real parameter $\zeta\ge0$. On the tensor product
$B_x^RB_s^R=B_x^R\otimes_SB_s^R$ define
$$L_\zeta:=(\rho\cdot(-))\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B_s^R}+\mathrm{id}_{B_x^R}\otimes(\zeta\,\rho\cdot(-)),$$
where the first summand is left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and
the second summand is left multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the second factor.
Because the polynomial ring is commutative and the balanced tensor product
identifies $b r\otimes c=b\otimes rc$ for $r\in S$, the second summand equals
right multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the first factor; both summands are
degree-two, $S$-linear on the right, and commute, so $L_\zeta$ is a degree-two
right-$S$-linear endomorphism of $B_x^RB_s^R$. In particular $L_\zeta$ preserves
the submodule $MS_+$ for $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$\mathbb R$-linear endomorphism of the reduced module
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ ([[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]
supplies the induced invariant form and the reduction conventions of
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]] apply).

**Symmetry.** Each summand of $L_\zeta$ is multiplication by an element in the
commutative position algebra of the tensor product: the first is multiplication
by $\rho$ on the first factor, the second is right (equivalently middle)
multiplication by $\zeta\rho$, which is self-adjoint for the induced invariant
form by the invariance identities of the form. Hence $L_\zeta$ is symmetric for
the induced form, and the Lefschetz forms $(\ ,\ )^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ and the
primitive subspaces $P^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ are those of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]] for this
operator.

**The deformation statements.** Write $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$,
$\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for centered hard
Lefschetz, the Hodge-Riemann relations and the strong embedded-form statement on
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ for the operator $L_\zeta$, with the bottom degree
$-\ell(x)-1$ and the standard sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ of the dictionary in
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]; the
definitions of $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form respectively to all choices of such forms.
At $\zeta=0$ the operator $L_0=\rho\cdot(-)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is left
multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor, so the zero-parameter statements
$\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ are exactly
the undeformed statements $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$,
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ of the dictionary. For fixed data the family
$\zeta\mapsto L_\zeta$ is polynomial of degree one in $\zeta$.

**Summand stability.** Any direct summand $B\subseteq B_x^RB_s^R$ that is a
sub-bimodule is stable under $L_0$, because left multiplication by the central
element $\rho$ is a bimodule endomorphism; stability under $L_\zeta$ for
$\zeta>0$ is a separate condition, since a projector onto $B$ need not commute
with the middle-position operator. The undeformed summand implications used in
the induction of this page are supplied by the local restriction lemma later on
this page, after deforming the parameter back to $\zeta=0$; no statement of this
definition identifies a restricted positive-parameter operator with a
restriction of $L_\zeta$.

Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. derivations.claim: **A genuine bimodule section.** Put $U=M\otimes_{S^s}S$, so $MB_s=U(1)$. The actual bimodule decomposition of [F1] gives $U\cong M\oplus M(-2)$. The multiplication counit $c:U\to M$, $c(b\otimes r)=br$, is an $S$-bimodule map. The bottom degree of $U$ is the single line $M^{-\ell(x)}\otimes1$, on which $c$ is nonzero. Only the unshifted summand $M$ in this decomposition has that degree, so $c$ restricts to a nonzero degree-zero endomorphism of that summand. By [F1] it is a nonzero scalar, hence invertible. Compose its inverse with the actual bimodule inclusion to obtain a degree-zero bimodule section $\sigma:M\to U$. On the bottom line $\sigma(b)=b\otimes1$, because $c\sigma=1$ and that line in $U$ is one dimensional.

**The twisted counit.** Define $c_s:U\to M_s$ by $c_s(b\otimes r)=b\,s(r)$. It is balanced over $S^s$, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. Since the section $\sigma$ in step 1.1 is genuinely right-$S$-linear, $t=c_s\sigma:M\to M$ is degree zero, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. It is the identity on the bottom line by step 1.1. This argument uses the actual bimodule summand, rather than the generally non-right-linear map $b\mapsto b\otimes1$.

**The involution property of $t$.** Since $t$ is right-$s$-semilinear and degree zero, $t^2$ is an ordinary degree-zero $S$-bimodule endomorphism of $M$, hence a scalar by $\operatorname{End}^0(M)=\mathbb R$; its scalar is $1$ because $t^2$ acts as the identity on the one-dimensional bottom degree by step 2.1. Hence $t^2=\mathrm{id}_M$.

**The descent isomorphism.** For $u\in U$ one has $c_s(u)-c(u)\in M\alpha_s$, because $s(r)-r\in\alpha_s S$ for every $r\in S$; consequently $t(m)-m\in M\alpha_s$ for every $m\in M$. Define $N:=\{m\in M: t(m)=m\}$. Every $m$ splits as $m=\tfrac12(m+t(m))+\tfrac12(m-t(m))$ into an invariant and an anti-invariant part, and an anti-invariant $m$ (that is, $t(m)=-m$) lies in $M\alpha_s$, say $m=n\alpha_s$; since right multiplication by $\alpha_s$ is injective by [F2] and $t(m)=-m$ with $s(\alpha_s)=-\alpha_s$ gives $t(n\alpha_s)=t(n)s(\alpha_s)=-t(n)\alpha_s$ and hence $t(n)=n$, we get $n\in N$ and the anti-invariant part of $m$ is $N\alpha_s$. Therefore $M=N\oplus N\alpha_s$ as $(S,S^s)$-bimodules, and the multiplication map induces an isomorphism $N\otimes_{S^s}S\to M$; this proves the descent isomorphism.

**The matrix of $L_\zeta$.** Use the proved descent $M=N\otimes_{S^s}S$ to write $MB_s=N\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$. Splitting the middle factor by $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ gives the bimodule isomorphism $MB_s\cong M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, with structure maps $\iota_1,\iota_2,\pi_1,\pi_2$ of [F2] satisfying $\pi_a\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$. In this basis, middle multiplication by $\rho$ has entries $\pi_1(\rho)$, $\pi_1(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and $\partial_s(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, and the operators of multiplication by $\rho$ on the two outer factors contribute the same diagonal $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$. All entries except the off-diagonal $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ have positive polynomial degree in $\rho$ and vanish after the right reduction; the off-diagonal entry has the constant term $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and contributes the degree-two map $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee):M(1)\to M(-1)$; hence, after reduction, $L_\zeta$ is the displayed matrix.

**Hard Lefschetz for $\zeta>0$.** Assume $\mathrm{hL}(x)$, so the reduced module $\overline M$ is a direct sum of centered $\rho$-strings $u_0,\ldots,u_m$ with $\deg u_j=-m+2j$ and $\rho u_j=u_{j+1}$; on each string, left multiplication by $\rho$ is the standard nilpotent Jordan block. In the two-dimensional middle factor with basis $v_-,v_+$ of degrees $-1,+1$ and $e(v_-)=\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)v_+$, $e(v_+)=0$, the operator $e=L_\zeta$ on the string tensor $\bigoplus_j u_j\otimes\{v_-,v_+\}$ acts by $e^k(u_jv_-)=u_{j+k}v_-+k\,u_{j+k-1}v_+$ and $e^k(u_jv_+)=u_{j+k}v_+$ (indices out of range zero), after normalizing the nonzero scalar $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ to $1$ by rescaling $v_+$; for $0\le k\le m-1$ of the compatible parity $k\equiv m+1\pmod2$, in centered degree $-k$ the source basis $u_{(m+1-k)/2}v_-,\,u_{(m-1-k)/2}v_+$ and the corresponding target basis exhibit $e^k$ as a matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and $1$, lower-left entry $k$, and upper-right entry $0$, which is invertible; at $k=m+1$ the map sends $u_0v_-$ to $(m+1)u_mv_+$, nonzero by the normalization $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$. The operator on each string is thus an isomorphism in every centered degree, and $L_\zeta$ on the direct sum of strings satisfies hL. Positivity of $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ uses $\zeta>0$ and strict dominance of $\rho$.

**Failure at $\zeta=0$ and conclusion.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of step 5.1 is diagonal with respect to the decomposition $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$. The bottom class $b\in\overline M^{-\ell(x)}$ sits in the first summand in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$ because $\overline M^{\ell(x)+2}=0$; the opposite class in $M(-1)$ of degree $\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality and dimension symmetry. Hence $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}$ is not injective on $\overline{MB_s}$ in the centered grading and centered hL fails at $\zeta=0$, even though the two individual shifted copies of $\overline M$ have their own strings centered at $\pm1$. Steps 1.1-5.1 prove the descent isomorphism and the matrix, step 6.1 the positive-parameter hard Lefschetz, and this step the failure at zero; no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$ is used.
